newsitem.title: NORWAY: Holbrooke urges Dayton-type talks after Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke urges Dayton-type talks after Bosnia poll.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. mediator who brokered the Bosnian peace deal, called on Thursday for a new Dayton-type conference after elections this month to promote democracy in the war-torn Balkan state.
Holbrooke said the international community should keep a reduced military presence in Bosnia after the NATO-led 60,000-strong peace mission ends by the end of the year.
Speaking at the Norwegian Nobel Foundation, Holbroke said his worst concern was that fascists or separatists opposed to the Dayton agreement would come to power in the September 14 vote.

"Whatever happens on September 14 I do not consider the game over," he said. "It's not like 'we had an election. It was free and fair, back to you'. That would be irresponsible. It would mean that European and American leaders have not learned the lessons of recent history."

The vote is the central plank in the implementation of the 1995 Dayton treaty which Holbrooke almost single-handedly negotiated as assistant U.S. secretary of state after years of hapless U.N. and European mediation.
Under the accords, the elections have to go ahead to put unified democratic institutions in place and allow NATO forces to go home.

But Holbrooke, now a Wall Street businessman, said: "The Dayton agreements were incomplete and inadequate and...there will have to be a second Dayton-type conference, not necessarily in Dayton, sometime later this year after the electons."

"And there will have to some form of international security presence in Bosnia next year. We can't just at the end of this year say 'well that is our year. Thank you, goodbye.' There has to be a transition.
"I hope that the next international conference will correct some of the mistakes we made at Dayton. The international police task force, for example, should be beefed up."
Human rights workers say conditions for a free and fair vote do not exist in Bosnia, but Holbrooke said:

"My concern is not the election itself. Supposing the election was declared free and fair and people are elected who are racists, fascists, separatists, who are publicly opposed to Dayton. That is the dilemma."
Holbooke said the so-called "Contact Group" -- the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Russia -- must hold the leaders to the Dayton agreement's terms for a single Bosnian state.

In July Holbrooke engineered the removal of Bosnian Serb separatist leader Radovan Karadzic, an indicted war criminal, from all public offices, but he said he was dissatisfied that Karadzic and his army commander Ratko Mladic had not been brought to trial.

"I am very well aware of the fact that Karadzic and Mladic and other war criminal are still at large," he said. "It makes me extremely upset. After the elections we have to get Karadzic either out of Pale or better yet move the capital of the Serb part of Bosnia from Pale to Banja Luka."

Suddenly the Nobel building was shaken by a large explosion, sending the crystal chandeliers clinking and the audience looking around nervously until someone said the blast was part of underground work on a tunnel.
"I thought Karadzic was here," quipped Holbrooke.
